summary: Describes mechanisms that let HTTP servers cryptographically bind security tokens such as cookies and OAuth tokens to TLS connections. It covers first-party and federated scenarios.

eli5.summary: Your login cookie gets stamped so it works only from your own connection, and a stolen cookie is useless.

questions: what is token binding over http
how does token binding stop cookie theft
subtitle: How browsers and servers carry Token Binding proofs in an HTTP header so stolen cookies and tokens stop working elsewhere.

tldr.problem: Cookies and OAuth tokens are bearer tokens: anyone who steals one can replay it from another machine. The Token Binding protocol defines a message that proves key possession, but not how to carry it in HTTP.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends a single Sec-Token-Binding request header holding a base64url-encoded TokenBindingMessage. For federated sign-on, a server can add Include-Referred-Token-Binding-ID: true to a redirect so the client also reveals the binding it uses with that server.
tldr.outcome: Servers can tie cookies and identity tokens to the client's key pair, so a replay over another connection is detectable. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and a companion to RFC 8471.

today: RFC 8473 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no replacement or update. It is a companion to RFC 8471.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 8471 defines a Token Binding ID for a TLS connection, built from the public key of a long-lived key pair whose private key the client proves it holds. A server that issues a security token, such as an HTTP cookie or an OAuth token, can put that ID inside the token and so bind it to connections from that particular client.

RFC 8471 defines a message format but not how it rides inside higher-level protocols. This RFC defines how a TokenBindingMessage is embedded in HTTP, both HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2. It only applies when HTTP runs over TLS (HTTPS), because token binding messages are only defined for TLS transports.
sections.eli5: A website can stamp your cookie with a secret mark that only your computer can match. This document says how your browser shows that mark to the website.

sections.title: The Sec-Token-Binding Header Field
sections.content:
Once client and server have negotiated Token Binding (see RFC 8471 and RFC 8472), the client MUST include exactly one Sec-Token-Binding header field in its HTTP requests. It MUST NOT appear in responses or in HTTP trailers. Its value is a base64url encoding of one TokenBindingMessage, with trailing = padding omitted and no line breaks or whitespace.

If a server receives more than one such header it MUST reject the request with 400 (Bad Request). The header SHOULD NOT be stored by origin servers on PUT requests and MAY be listed in a Vary response header. In HTTP/2 the client SHOULD use header compression so the repeated header is cheap.

The message MUST contain exactly one TokenBinding of type provided_token_binding, signed with the key pair the client uses with the server receiving the request. If validation fails, any tokens bound to that binding MUST also be rejected. The server may answer 400, give an application-specific "invalid token" response, or close the connection.
sections.eli5: Every time your browser asks for a page, it holds up one small signed note that says who it is. If a request holds up two notes, the website says no.

sections.title: Scoping of Key Pairs
sections.content:
For binding cookies, a browser's Token Binding key pair MUST be no wider than a registered domain (also called eTLD+1). For https://www.example.com the public suffix is com and the registered domain is example.com. User agents SHOULD use an up-to-date public suffix list.

In practice a key pair is therefore never scoped wider than a cookie that a browser would allow. If a browser limits cookies more narrowly, key pairs MAY be narrower too. Keys that bind other tokens, such as OAuth tokens or OpenID Connect ID Tokens, SHOULD follow the same rule, while non-browser applications MAY use different scoping.
sections.eli5: Your browser keeps one secret stamp per website family, not one for the whole internet. That way a stamp that works for one family is not shared with strangers.

sections.title: Renegotiation and First-Party Use
sections.content:
Token Binding over HTTP/1.1 can be used with TLS renegotiation, but only if renegotiation happens between a request and the server's response, the client sends no pipelined requests, and the client never starts renegotiation itself. These rules let both sides know which TLS Exported Keying Material value was signed, and stop a message from being split across a renegotiation boundary. The RFC notes it deals with TLS 1.2 and points to a separate document for TLS 1.3.

In the first-party (same-site) case, a server issues a token such as a cookie and expects it back later, for example to authenticate. Binding it to the TLS connection lets the server notice if the token is replayed over other connections.
sections.eli5: If a website only talks to you and gives you a ticket, it can check that the ticket is shown by the same person it was given to.

sections.title: Federation and Referred Bindings
sections.content:
Normally a client uses a different key pair for each server, for privacy. That stops a server from binding a token to a connection the client has with another server, which federated sign-on needs: an Identity Provider wants to bind an identity token to the client's connection with a Relying Party. The RFC calls the server that asks for the token the Token Consumer and the one that issues it the Token Provider.

When a Token Consumer redirects the client to a Token Provider, it SHOULD add the response header Include-Referred-Token-Binding-ID: true (the value is case insensitive). The client then adds a second TokenBinding, of type referred_token_binding, to the request to the Token Provider, signed with the key it uses with the Token Consumer. The provided binding (for the Token Provider) is still required.

The header only means something on redirect responses (300-399) to a request that carried Sec-Token-Binding; otherwise the client MUST ignore it. The referred binding goes only in the first request after that response, and is sent even if both servers share the same eTLD+1. Without the header, the client discloses nothing about its binding with the Token Consumer.
sections.eli5: If a school sends you to the library, the school can tell your phone to show the librarian your school ID stamp too. Without that note, your phone keeps the stamp private.

sections.title: Chains, Key Parameters and the OpenID Example
sections.content:
The RFC gives a non-normative redirect-chain approach: the Token Consumer redirects to Token Provider TP1, which adds the same header and redirects to TP2. TP2 issues a token bound to the client's binding with TP1, and TP1 then issues one for the Token Consumer bound to the referred binding it received earlier.

The client MUST use the key parameters it negotiated with the Token Consumer in the referred binding, even if they differ from those used with the receiving server. A Token Provider SHOULD support all key parameters in RFC 8471, and if it does not support those in the referred binding it MUST NOT issue a bound token.

The worked example is an OpenID Connect redirect sign-on. In step 0 the client establishes binding TBID1 with the Token Consumer. In steps 1a and 1b it is redirected to the Token Provider and sends both a provided binding (TBID2) and a referred binding (TBID1). In steps 3a and 3b the Token Provider returns an ID Token containing TBID1, and the client delivers it back to the Token Consumer.
sections.eli5: Each stop on the trip stamps the pass with the right mark, so at the end the first place can check the pass really came back through you.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An attacker can only replay a bound token from another machine if they also export the matching private key, so these keys SHOULD be strongly protected, ideally in a hardware security module that prevents export. The header also needs integrity: a client must not be tricked into sending a Token Binding signed by a key it does not control, which could make it log in to an attacker's account. One eTLD+1 should not be able to set the header used for another, and the Sec- prefix helps by marking it a forbidden header name for scripts.

In federation both proofs are needed. A man-in-the-middle between client and Token Provider is caught by the provided binding. One between client and Token Consumer is defeated because the referred binding travels in the header, which that attacker cannot alter the way it can alter redirect URLs. Token Providers and Consumers must still do their usual checks, such as identifying consumers and verifying the audience of tokens.
sections.eli5: The secret stamp is only safe if no one copies it. If a thief copies your stamp, the lock cannot tell the thief from you.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Clients use different key pairs for different servers so that Token Binding does not become a tracking tool. Because the key pairs have no expiry, they could track a user like a long-lived cookie, so web user agents SHOULD offer a way to discard them, and MUST discard them after a private browsing session if cookies are discarded there.

Revealing a referred Token Binding ID can expose a correlation handle linking two servers. Implementations MUST only convey IDs to servers when the application signals them to, and unrelated applications on the same system should not see each other's bindings.
sections.eli5: A stamp that lasts forever could let people follow you around. So you should be able to throw your stamps away, just like deleting cookies.
